newsitem.title: UK: Gazprom ADS hit by rule change, bond talk.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom ADS hit by rule change, bond talk.

text.p: American Depositary Shares (ADS) in Russian gas giant RAO Gazprom fell 65 cents to $17.00/$17.25 by 1030 GMT after the company late on Wednesday announced changes to its share structure, on talk of a bond issue and a large U.S. bank flattening its books, traders said.
"The changes to the rules make the ADS in Gazprom look expensive if the company is going to widen share trading," said an east European share trader in London.
Russia's Federal Securities Commission said on Wednesday the company would ease controls over its shares by not exercising its first refusal to buy stock, which has stymied liquidity.
The local stock was quoted at 41 cents in Moscow on Thursday and each ADS represents 10 underlying shares.

"People are wondering what will happen if the company issues a convertible bond, do they want to hold that in preference to the ADS and also about new overseas share issues by Gazprom," said the trader.

The $430 million Gapzrom raised from enthusiastic foreign investors via the ADS issue at $15.75 apiece three weeks ago was just the start of a massive programme to part-fund its $40 billion capital expenditure over the next 10 years.
The company has said it is considering a euro or a convertible bond issue and plans to sell up to nine percent of its capital overseas once it has completed accounts to U.S. standards.
Traders also said that a large seller of Gazprom ADS had emerged and a major U.S. bank was looking to square its books ahead of the weekend.
"Gazprom ADS is a long term investment, but with the market having risen so much, people are looking to take profits," said a trader.
Investors are also sceptical of reports of the rapid recovery of Russian President Boris Yeltsin from his heart operation on Tuesday.

"That a man who had a quintuple bypass is now signing decrees is difficult to believe, all the information is coming from Kremlin spokesmen and there has been no sign of Yeltsin himself," said the trader.
Fund managers agree, and one manager at a European bank noted that he would be neutral to underweight on the blue chips in the Russian market over the short to medium term.
"The market has had a hell of a rise and all the funds who have been there are in good shape so no one is looking to buy before Christmas," he said.
He noted that for investors wanting exposure to Russia, there was much better value in second-line stocks. -- David Chance London newsroom 44 171 542 5887
